# The Yorkshire Three Peaks: a 8-week plan (starter start)

*Generated by the Don't Die Retired guidance engine on 27 October 2026 from 26 sourced statements. Draft for review: not yet checked by a coach, physiotherapist or doctor.*

## The challenge

24 miles (38.6 km) with about 5,000 feet (1,600 m) of climbing over Pen-y-Ghent, Ingleborough and Whernside, usually in one day. [1, 2]

## Before you start

- If you have a health condition or are worried about your health, speak to your GP (family doctor) before you start training. [3, 4]
- Start from your current level and build up gradually; repeating a week is fine and is part of the plan, not a failure. [3, 5]

> **This plan is too short for your starting point.** From this starting point the long session would have to grow by about 65 per cent a week, more than this plan allows. Choose more weeks, or a lower first goal, before you start.

## How the plan works

- Do most of your training at an easy, conversational effort, about 2 to 3 out of 10, where you could hold a full conversation. Keep a small share for harder work. [6, 7, 8]
- Increase your training a little at a time. Big week-to-week jumps (more than about 30 per cent) were linked with more overuse injuries in a study of 874 new runners; the familiar 10 per cent rule is a sensible cap but is not firmly proven. [3, 9]
- Build one long session a week at an easy effort, growing towards the length and duration of the challenge itself. [2, 8]
- Train for the ground you will cover. For hill challenges walk hills fast, or use stairs, and add short hill repeats of 50 to 100 metres of climb, four to six times, coming down slowly. [1, 2]
- Know the real demands of your challenge (distance, total climb, time on your feet, altitude) and make sure your plan builds towards them. [1, 2]
- Plan rest days into every week, and take an easier day when your legs are heavy. [3, 8, 10]
- Do strength exercises for the whole body on at least two days a week. In trials, strength training cut sports injuries to about a third. [2, 5, 11]
- In the later weeks, train with the pack and the kit you will carry on the day so nothing is new. [1, 2]
- In the final two weeks, cut your training volume by roughly 40 to 60 per cent while keeping the same number of sessions and some of the same effort, so you arrive fresh. [8, 12, 13]

## Week by week

Rest on Mondays and Fridays. Strength and balance (about 30 minutes, routine below) on Wednesdays and Sundays. The Saturday long hill walk is the key session: on hilly ground where you can, building the climbing as well as the hours.

| Week | Tue | Thu | Sat: long hill walk | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | 2 hours |  |
| 2 | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | 2.5 hours |  |
| 3 | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | hill repeats | 2 hours | easier week |
| 4 | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | hill repeats | 3 hours | start carrying your loaded pack on the long session |
| 5 | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | hill repeats | 3.5 hours |  |
| 6 | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | hill repeats | 3 hours | easier week |
| 7 | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | brisk walk, 45 min, easy | 5.5 hours | taper begins: same sessions, less of each |
| 8 | brisk walk, 20 min, easy | rest | **the challenge** | event week: rest, sleep, eat well |

*Hill repeats*: climb a steep road, hill or stairs for 50 to 100 metres of height, four to six times, coming down slowly. [1, 2]

## Looking after your body

- Include balance work; for older adults the official guidance pairs it with strength on two days a week, and balance (proprioception) training also reduced injuries in trials. [5, 11]
- Stretch after a long day if it feels good, but do not rely on stretching to prevent injury; trials found it made no difference, unlike strength and balance work. [2, 11]
- Weight-bearing activity such as walking and running helps keep bones strong. [5]
- Keep a regular sleep routine through training; good sleep is part of recovery, and on multi-day trips a warm enough sleeping bag and mat matter more than people expect. [10, 13]
- If you miss a session, do not worry about it; carry on with the plan, or repeat a week if you need to. [3, 13]

**Strength and balance routine (twice a week).** Squats, lunges, a core exercise such as a plank, and a balance exercise such as standing on one leg. Start with your own body weight, two sets of 8 to 12 slow repetitions, and add load only when that feels easy. [2, 5, 11]

## Fuel, drink and feet

- Train in the footwear you will use on the day and break new shoes in gradually. Wear moisture-wicking socks and change them if your feet sweat. [10, 13, 14]
- Deal with a hot spot as soon as you feel it. Cover a blister with a soft or padded plaster and do not burst it; get advice if it shows signs of infection. [10, 14]

## Kit for the day

Rucksack with dry bags, worn-in boots, layers, waterproofs, hat, gloves, spare warm clothes, food, water, map (OS Explorer OL2), compass, whistle, first aid kit, sun protection, torch with spare batteries, charged phone, emergency shelter, poles if you use them. [1, 2]

## On the day

- Carry a map and compass and know how to use them; do not rely on signs or a phone, whose signal and battery can fail. [1, 2]
- Start slower than you think you need to; early miles feel easy and are where most people overdo it. [6, 13]

## Safety

- Drink when you are thirsty rather than to a schedule. Drinking far more than you need can dilute the body's sodium, which can be dangerous; it affects walkers and recreational exercisers as well as racers. [15]
- Check the forecast, walk in daylight, leave your route with someone, and turn back if conditions get beyond you. Summits are colder than valleys. [1]
- Call 999 (911 in the US) for tight or squeezing chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw, severe breathlessness, or if someone collapses. Do not drive yourself to hospital. [16]
- Stop if something does not feel right, and get it checked rather than training through it. [3, 13]
